summary: Updates the 6LoWPAN extensions to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery so a listener can subscribe to an IPv6 anycast or multicast address. It also updates RPL with a new Non-Storing multicast mode and support for anycast addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: Small battery-powered devices sleep to save power, so they cannot shout questions to everybody on the network the way ordinary IPv6 does. This document lets a sleeping device quietly tell its router which group addresses it wants to hear, and the router announces that address once for the whole network.

questions: how to subscribe to ipv6 multicast in 6lowpan
what is the p-field in earo
subtitle: Lets a sleeping low-power node subscribe to an IPv6 multicast or anycast address through its router.

tldr.problem: Classical IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Multicast Listener Discovery work by multicasting queries to every node on the link. On a low-power network where nodes sleep most of the time, that wakes everyone up for a question meant for one node.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a subscription to the 6LoWPAN registration mechanism: a node sends a Neighbor Solicitation with an Extended Address Registration Option whose new 2-bit P-Field says the address is multicast or anycast. The router keeps one registration per subscriber and advertises the address once into RPL, with a new Mode of Operation 5 for Non-Storing networks.
tldr.outcome: A listener can join a group or an anycast service without speaking RPL, which also keeps it out of the routing protocol and so out of reach of several attacks. Delivery is still not guaranteed exactly once, so upper layer protocols must tolerate loss and duplication.

today: RFC 9685 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2024. It updates RFC 4861, RFC 6550, RFC 6553, RFC 8505 and RFC 9010, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Sleepy Nodes Need Another Way
sections.content:
The design of Low-Power and Lossy Networks is generally focused on saving energy, which is the most constrained resource of all. Other design constraints, such as limited memory capacity, duty cycling of the devices and low-power lossy transmissions, derive from that primary concern. The radio, when transmitting or simply listening, is a major energy drain, and the protocols must let the nodes sleep with the radio turned off at most times.

RPL provides IPv6 routing within those constraints. To save signalling and routing state, the routing is performed only along a Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph (DODAG) optimized to reach a Root node, rather than along the shortest path between two peers, and broken routes may be fixed lazily and on demand when the data plane reveals an inconsistency.

The classical Neighbor Discovery protocol was defined for serial links and shared transit media such as Ethernet, at a time when broadcast on those media was cheap while memory for a neighbour cache was expensive. It was designed as a reactive protocol relying on caching and multicast operations for address discovery and duplicate address detection. Those multicast operations typically affect every node on the link when at most one is really targeted, which is a waste of energy and implies that all nodes are awake to hear the request, which is inconsistent with sleeping modes.

RFC 6775 changed the model so that a node proactively establishes the neighbour cache entry for its unicast address in the routers that serve it, using a new Address Registration Option in unicast Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages. RFC 8505 turned that into a generic registration mechanism and introduced the Extended Address Registration Option, giving a routing-agnostic way for a host to ask the router to inject its unicast address into the local routing protocol. RFC 9010 provides the router counterpart for RPL. MLDv2 lets the router learn who listens to which multicast address, but it also relies on multicasting queries to all nodes, which is unfit for low-power operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary IPv6 asks the whole room a question when it needs to reach one person. On a network of sleeping sensors, that wakes every sensor. The fix is for the sensor to tell its router directly, one unicast message at a time.

sections.title: Registration Becomes Subscription
sections.content:
This specification extends RFC 8505 with a registration method, called subscription, for anycast and multicast addresses, and inherits the proof of ownership defined in RFC 8928 that already protects the registration in RFC 8505. RFC 8505 is agnostic to the routing protocol in which the address may be redistributed.

As opposed to unicast addresses, there might be multiple registrations from multiple parties for the same address. The router retains one registration per party for each multicast or anycast address but injects the route into the routing protocol only once for each address, and the injection happens asynchronously to the registration. The validation exchange with the registrar is still needed if the router checks the right of the host to listen to the address.

The flow is the one of Figure 1. The 6LoWPAN Node sends a Neighbor Solicitation carrying an Extended Address Registration Option to its 6LoWPAN Router. The router validates it with the 6LoWPAN Border Router, acting as registrar, using an Extended Duplicate Address Request and an Extended Duplicate Address Confirmation, then replies with a Neighbor Advertisement carrying the same option and injects the route. Because several nodes may subscribe the same address, the border router receives and accepts multiple Extended Duplicate Address Requests for the same address, and the address being registered by multiple nodes is not treated as a duplication.

The EARO gains a new 2-bit field, the P-Field, which signals that the registration is for a multicast address (1) or an anycast address (2). The existing R flag that requests reachability for the registered address gets new behaviour: when it is set in the subscription of one or more nodes for the same address, the router injects the anycast addresses and the multicast addresses of a scope larger than link scope into RPL, based on the longest subscription lifetime across the active subscriptions for that address. The use of the term subscribe is deliberate: a node registers the unicast addresses that it owns but subscribes to the multicast addresses that it listens to.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks with the border router that the subscription is legitimate, then tells the rest of the network once that the address has a listener. Several devices may want the same group address, and that is not an error.

sections.title: The P-Field and Its Values
sections.content:
The new Registered Address Type Indicator is created for use in the RPL Target Option, the Extended Address Registration Option and the header of Extended Duplicate Address Request messages. It indicates whether an address is unicast, multicast or anycast, and the new 2-bit P-Field transports it in the different protocols.

The P-Field is set to 0 for a unicast registration, 1 for a multicast registration and 2 for an anycast registration. The value 3 is intended for a prefix registration, expected in a later specification. RPL already advertises prefixes and treats unicast addresses as prefixes of length 128, so it does not need that new value, but 6LoWPAN ND does, so the value will not be processed adequately: when it is received in an RPL Target Option it must be ignored, meaning it is treated as 0, while the message is processed normally, and in an EARO or an EDAR the message must be dropped, with the receiving node optionally replying with a status of 12, Invalid Registration, or remaining silent.

The field is placed in three places. In the EARO it sits at position 2 of the 8-bit flags array, and a new 2-bit reserved field takes the two bits above it, which must be set to zero and ignored by the receiver. In the EDAR message the reserved Status field is repurposed as a Flags field, and the P-Field sits at position 0 of that array with a 6-bit reserved field above it. The EDAC message is not modified. In the RPL Target Option the P-Field is placed at bits 2 to 3, where the flags at positions 0 and 1 are already defined.
sections.plainLanguage: A two-bit label on each registration says what kind of address it is: one receiver, a group, or whichever helper is closest. A fourth value is reserved for a future case and is refused.

sections.title: What Changes in RPL
sections.content:
The specification amends RFC 6550 to mandate the use of the ROVR field as the indication of the origin of a Target advertisement in RPL DAO messages. For anycast and multicast advertisements multiple origins may subscribe to the same address, in which case the advertisements are merged by the common parent, which becomes the origin of the merged advertisements and uses its own ROVR value; a parent that propagates an advertisement from a single origin uses the original ROVR. The Path Sequence freshness comparison is used only between advertisements for the same Target from the same origin.

The router that merges multiple advertisements for the same address must use and advertise the longest remaining lifetime across all the origins, and when that lifetime expires it sends a no-path DAO message with a lifetime of 0, using the same ROVR value as for the previous advertisements.

A new Mode of Operation 5 adds Non-Storing mode with ingress replication multicast support. The DAO messages announce the multicast addresses as Targets and never as Transits, and the Root performs the ingress replication: it transmits one copy of each multicast packet to each 6LR that is a transit for the multicast target, using the same source-routing header and encapsulation as it would for a unicast packet for a RPL-Unaware Leaf attached to that 6LR. For intermediate routers the packet appears as any source-routed unicast packet, and the difference shows only at the 6LR, which terminates the source-routed path and forwards the multicast packet to all the nodes that registered for the multicast address.

Anycast addresses can be injected in RPL in both Storing and Non-Storing modes. A target is routed as anycast by a parent or the Root that received at least one DAO message for that target with the P-Field set to 2. When forwarding multicast packets down the DODAG, the router copies all the children that advertised the address; when forwarding anycast packets down, it must copy one and only one of those children. The anycast operation applies to both addresses and prefixes, and an external destination that may be injected as an RPL Target from multiple border routers should be injected as anycast to enable load balancing.
sections.plainLanguage: For a group address the router sends copies down every branch that has a listener. For an anycast address it picks exactly one branch, which is how the traffic is shared out between several helpers.

sections.title: The Rules a Node and a Router Follow
sections.content:
The node must subscribe all the IPv6 multicast addresses that it listens to and set the P-Field to 1 in the EARO for them, with one exception: the all-nodes link-scope multicast address ff02::1 is implicitly registered by all nodes, which are expected to accept messages sent to it but are not expected to register it. The node must also subscribe all the IPv6 anycast addresses that it supports and set the P-Field to 2.

The P-Field is not consistent with the registered address if the address is a multicast address and the P-Field indicates a value other than 1, or if the address is not a multicast address and the P-Field indicates 1. In that case the message must be dropped, and the receiving node may reply with a status of 12, Invalid Registration, or stay silent. The node may set the R flag in the EARO to obtain delivery of the multicast packets by the router, for example through MLD proxy operations or by injecting the address into a route-over subnet or into PIM.

The router and the border router are extended to accept more than one subscription for the same address when it is anycast or multicast, since multiple nodes may subscribe to the same address of these types. The ROVR in the EARO uniquely identifies a registration within the namespace of the registered address. The router must maintain a subscription state per tuple of IPv6 address and ROVR, and should notify the border router with an EDAR message unless it has determined that the border router is legacy.

A router that wishes to refresh its state, for example after a reboot, should send an asynchronous NA(EARO) with the new status 11, Registration Refresh Request. That multicast message must be sent to the all-nodes link-scope address ff02::1, with the Target set to the link-local address that the node exposed previously. The TID follows the lollipop rules, so a TID below 128 must not be taken as a reboot. The request may be reissued a few times to increase the chances of delivery, with the TID incremented each time, and the receiver must process one and only one of the series. By default the initial TID after boot is 252, the SEQUENCE_WINDOW is 4, the short period is 10 seconds, the interval between retries is 1 second and the number of retries is 3.
sections.plainLanguage: A device tells the router which group and anycast addresses it wants, and says in the same message whether it wants the traffic actually routed to it. If the router loses its memory after a restart, it asks everyone to sign up again, and each device answers once.

sections.title: What the Router Does With the Subscription
sections.content:
RFC 9010 had no procedure for the router to inject multicast and anycast routes in RPL, and only injected a unicast address into the RPL unicast support when a registration carried the R flag set to 1. This specification extends it.

Upon a subscription with the R flag and the P-Field both set to 1 in the EARO, and if the scope of the multicast address is above link scope, the router injects the address in the RPL multicast support and sets the P-Field in the RTO to 1 as well. Upon a subscription with the R flag set to 1 and the P-Field set to 2, the router injects the address in the new RPL anycast support and sets the P-Field to 2 in the RTO.

On the way back, when the router receives a packet directed to a multicast address for which it has at least one subscription, it delivers a copy of the packet as a unicast Layer 2 frame to the link-layer address of each of the nodes that registered to that multicast address. When the packet is directed to an anycast address, it delivers a copy to exactly one of the nodes that registered to it.

Delivering each copy as a unicast frame matters on these links. LLN links are typically Direct MAC Broadcast with no emulation to increase range or reliability; in such links broadcasting is unreliable and asynchronous transmissions force a listener to remain awake, so asynchronous broadcasting is generally inefficient. The expectation is that whenever possible the routers deliver the multicast packets as individual unicast frames to each of the nodes that subscribed.
sections.plainLanguage: When the traffic arrives, the router sends each interested device its own copy, addressed directly to it, rather than shouting it to the whole radio range and waking everyone.

sections.title: Getting This Into a Running Network
sections.content:
With this specification a RPL DODAG forms a realm, and multiple DODAGs may be federated in a single RPL Instance administratively. A multicast address that needs to span a DODAG must use a Realm-Local scope, and one that needs to span an RPL Instance must use an Admin-Local scope.

The new Mode of Operation 5 cannot be deployed by updating a live network. The administrator must create a new instance with MOP 5 and migrate nodes to it by allowing them to join it. In a green field deployment where all nodes support this specification, a single RPL Instance using a multicast MOP can serve unicast, multicast and anycast addresses. In a brown field where legacy devices coexist with upgraded ones, it is RECOMMENDED to deploy one RPL Instance, typically MOP 1, for unicast that legacy nodes can join, and a separate instance dedicated to multicast and anycast operations using a multicast MOP.

Deploying Storing mode multicast with MOP 3 requires the routers that support MOP 3 to have enough density to build a DODAG that covers all potential listeners and the spanning multicast trees needed to distribute the flows, which may not be the case when extending an existing network. For the new Non-Storing multicast MOP, the support is only needed at the 6LRs that will accept multicast listeners, so the upgraded routers must be deployed to cover all the nodes that need multicast services.

Using separate instances for unicast on one hand and anycast and multicast on the other allows different objective functions, one favouring the link quality up for unicast collection and the other favouring downwards link quality for multicast distribution. A mixed mode is also allowed, signalled as MOP 1 in the DIO messages for backward compatibility, where the MOP signalled is MOP 1 so that legacy nodes can operate as leaves, and the support of multicast and anycast should be signalled to the nodes by the routers using the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option.
sections.plainLanguage: A new mode of operation cannot be switched on in a running network. The administrator builds a second network that uses it and moves devices over, while the old devices carry on in the old one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The specification extends RFC 8505 and RFC 9010 and leverages RFC 9008, so the security sections of those documents apply. In particular the link layer should be sufficiently protected to prevent rogue access.

RPL already supports routing on multicast addresses, whereby the endpoint that subscribes to the group by injecting the multicast address participates in the RPL as a RPL-Aware Node. Using an extension of RFC 8505 instead of RPL to subscribe allows a RPL-Unaware Leaf to subscribe as well, which gives a better security posture for the network: nodes that do not need to speak RPL, or are not trusted enough to inject RPL messages, can be forbidden from doing so, which bars a number of attack vectors from within RPL.

Compared to RFC 6550, this specification enables tracking the origin of a multicast subscription inside the RPL network, which is a first step towards a form of Route Ownership Validation using the ROVR field in the EARO as proof of ownership. RFC 8928 protects the ownership of unicast addresses, but anycast and multicast addresses are not owned by one node, so the mechanism cannot be used with autoconfigured key pairs to protect a single ownership. A key pair must still be associated with the address before it is deployed, and a ROVR generated from that key pair must be installed in the border router so it can recognize the address and compare the ROVR on the first subscription, and the key pair must be provisioned in each node that needs to subscribe. How the ROVR values are distributed is out of scope; one way would be to authorize the ROVR of the valid users in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: A device that only wants to receive group traffic never has to speak the routing protocol, so it cannot attack the routing protocol. The document also points at how a group address could later be tied to a key.
